source_text: ἀδόκιμον, ἀχάριστον καὶ βέβηλον ἐξ οἰκείας γνώμης φανέν, γραφῆς δὲ μήτε λεγούσης εἶναι τοῦ θεϊκοῦ πνεύματος ἀρχήν, «πνεῦμα δὲ τοῦ θεοῦ» καὶ «ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ» καὶ «θεῖον» καὶ «ἅγιον» εὐφημούσης αὐτό, μήτε δὲ ἀφοριζούσης ἐπὶ τῆς φύσεως τῶν θείων ὑποστάσεως τὸ πρώτιστα καὶ τὸ ἔπειτα, ποῖα περὶ τοῦ εἶναι αὐτὰς ἐν τῇ ἀγενήτῳ μιᾷ θεότητι καὶ ἰσοτιμίᾳ ὑπολείπεται ἀμφισβήτησις; 6.2ν ὅτι πληροῖ τὴν οἰκουμένην, καὶ συνέχει τὰ πάντα οὐδὲν κτιστὸν πληροῖ τὴν οἰκουμένην, ἢ συνέχει τὰ πάντα, καὶ ἐν πᾶσιν τυγχάνει· ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν νοερῶν δυνάμεων πέρας 55 ἐστίν, καὶ ὡρισμένη ποσότης· μόνως γὰρ ταῦτα τῆς θεότητος ἴδια. ἡ δὲ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος μεγαλοσύνη ἀδιάλυτος, ἀπέραντος καὶ πανταχοῦ καὶ διὰ πάντων καὶ ἐν πᾶσιν ἀεί ἐστιν· πληροῦσα μὲν τὸν κόσμον καὶ συνέχουσα κατὰ τὴν θεότητα, ἀχώρητος δὲ κατὰ τὴν δύναμιν, καὶ μετροῦσα μέν, οὐ μετρουμένη δέ. «οὐ γὰρ ἐκ μέτρου δίδωσιν ὁ θεὸς τὸ πνεῦμα,» ὡς ὁ σωτὴρ ἐν Ἰωάννῃ λέγει· καὶ κατὰ τὴν Σοφίαν, ἔχουσαν· «ἀγαπᾷς γὰρ τὰ ὄντα πάντα, καὶ οὐδὲν βδελύσσῃ, ὧν ἐποίησας· οὐδὲ γὰρ ἂν μισῶν τι κατεσκεύασας. πῶς δὲ ἔμεινεν ἄν τι, εἰ μὴ σὺ ἠθέλησας ἢ τὸ μὴ βληθὲν ὑπὸ σοῦ ἐτηρήθη; φείδῃ δὲ πάν των, ὅτι πάντα σά ἐστιν, δέσποτα φιλόψυχε, καὶ τὸ ἄφθαρτόν σου πνεῦμά ἐστιν ἐν πᾶσιν.» ἔνθεν καὶ πατέρα πάντων τὸν θεὸν εἰκότως ὀνομάζομεν, οὐκ ὄντα ἡμῶν φύσει πατέρα, ὡς ἔστιν τοῦ μονογενοῦς αὐτοῦ. καὶ πάλιν· «πνεῦμα κυρίου πεπλήρωκεν τὴν οἰκουμένην, καὶ τὸ συνέχον τὰ πάντα γνῶσιν ἔχει φωνῆς·» ἀντὶ τοῦ περιέλαβεν τὴν ἀόρατον καὶ ὁρατὴν κτίσιν, τὴν νοητὴν καὶ αἰσθητήν, καὶ οὐδὲν τῶν πάντων ἐστὶν ἄμοιρον τῆς ἀιδίου ἐπιστασίας αὐτοῦ· τὸ γὰρ πάντα συνέχειν τοῦτο δηλοῖ. καὶ πάσης, φησίν, ἐπακούει φωνῆς, ὡς θεὸς ἐν πᾶσιν πανταχοῦ ἀεὶ τυγχάνων, καὶ πᾶσαν ὑλικὴν ἀναρμοστίαν εἰς τάξιν περιάγων τὴν πρέπουσαν, καὶ τῶν πρὸς αὐτοῦ ποιηθέντων φειδόμενός τε καὶ ἐπιμελούμενος, ἅτε αὐτὸς τὴν φύσιν πρόνοια ὑπάρχων καὶ σοφία, δι' ὅλων διαπεφοιτηκυῖα, ὡς ὁ πατήρ. τίς γὰρ ὁ τοιαύτην ἔχων γνῶσιν; Ἡσαῖάς τε λέγει οὕτως· «πνεῦμα γνώσεως καὶ εὐσεβείας,» καὶ ὁ ∆αυὶδ προσᾴδει· «ποῦ πορευθῶ ἀπὸ τοῦ προσώπου σου; καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ πνεύματός σου ποῦ φύγω;» καὶ ὁ δεσπότης δὲ διδάσκων, ὡς ἡ θεότης τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος οὐ περιγράφεται τόπῳ, ἀλλ' ὁμοῦ ἐν οὐρανῷ τέ ἐστιν καὶ ἐπὶ γῆς, πᾶσαν αὐτάρκειαν παρασχόμενον ἀεὶ καὶ παρεχόμενον τῇ κτίσει, ἔφη παρ' Ἰωάννῃ· «ἐὰν ἀγαπᾶτέ με, τὰς ἐντολὰς τὰς ἐμὰς τηρήσατε· κἀγὼ ἐρω τήσω τὸν πατέρα, καὶ ἄλλον παράκλητον δώσει ὑμῖν, ἵνα ᾖ μεθ' ὑμῶν τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς ἀληθείας, ὃ ὁ κόσμος οὐ δύναται λαβεῖν, οὐ θεωρεῖ αὐτὸ οὐδὲ γινώσκει αὐτό· ὑμεῖς δὲ γινώσκετε αὐτὸ, ὅτι παρ' ὑμῖν μένει, καὶ ἐν ὑμῖν ἔσται.» ἵνα δὲ γνώριμον γένηται, ὡς τῆς πανταχοῦ παρούσης μιᾶς ἀπείρου φύσεως καὶ αἱ τοιαίδε μαρτυρίαι ἀποφαίνουσιν αὐτό· τὰ ἴσα παρέδοσαν περὶ ἑκατέρας ἀκηράτου ὑποστάσεως, Ἰερεμίας μὲν ἐξηγούμενος ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ πατρός· «τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν ἐγὼ πληρῶ, λέγει κύριος·» ∆αυὶδ δὲ περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ ἐν ρμδʹ ψαλμῷ κελαδῶν· «καὶ τῆς μεγαλοσύνης αὐτοῦ οὐκ ἔστιν πέρας·» Παῦλος δὲ κηρύττων περὶ τοῦ αὐτοῦ· «ὁ καταβὰς αὐτός ἐστιν καὶ ὁ ἀναβὰς ὑπὲρ ἄνω πάντων τῶν οὐρανῶν, ἵνα πληρώσῃ τὰ πάντα.» 6.3ν ὅτι ἄφθαρτον ἡ κτίσις οὐκ ἄφθαρτος καθάπαξ ἐστίν· ἀλλὰ φθορὰν ἐπιδέχεται, τὴν τροφήν, ἥν φαμεν καὶ μεταβολήν, ὡς ἡ προφητεία λέγει· «ὁ ποιῶν πάντα καὶ μετασκευάζων αὐτά.» ἧς κατακούσαντες τῶν ἔξω σοφοί, φασίν· αὐτὰ λύων εἰς αὐτά, καὶ ἐξ αὐτῶν πάλιν αὔξων. ἡμὲν γὰρ ἀσώματος λογικὴ κτίσις τὴν κατὰ προαίρεσιν ἔχει φθοράν, τοῦ μὲν θεοῦ μόνιμον αὐτῇ φύσιν δεδωκότος, καὶ στήσαντος αὐτὴν εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα, καὶ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τοῦ αἰῶνος· αὐτῆς δὲ αὐτοπροαιρέτως μεταβαλλομένης, καὶ εἰς χείρονα ἐκπιπτούσης λῆξιν, καὶ αὐτῷ
pass_a_gloss: [...] unapproved, ungrateful and profane, having appeared such out of its own judgement. And Scripture neither saying that there is a beginning of the divine Spirit, but speaking well of him as 'Spirit of God' and 'out of God' and 'divine' and 'holy', nor marking off upon the nature of the divine hypostases the 'first of all' and the 'after', what sort of dispute is left over about their being in the unbegotten one Godhead and equality of honour? 6.2ν [Chapter title:] That he fills the inhabited world and holds together all things. Nothing created fills the inhabited world, or holds together all things, and happens to be in all things; but even of the intellectual powers there is a limit (printed page 55 here) and a defined quantity; for these things are the Godhead's own alone. But the greatness of the Holy Spirit is undissolvable, limitless, and is always everywhere and through all things and in all things: filling the world and holding it together according to the Godhead, but uncontainable according to the power, and measuring, but not being measured. 'For not out of measure does God give the Spirit', as the Saviour says in John; and according to the Wisdom, which has: 'for you love all the things that are, and you loathe nothing of the things you made; for you would not have fashioned anything hating it. And how would anything have remained, if you had not willed, or what was not called (copy-text: thrown) by you have been kept? And you spare all things, because all things are yours, Master who loves souls, and your incorruptible Spirit is in all things.' From there also we fittingly name God father of all, he not being our father by nature, as he is of his Only-begotten. And again: 'the Spirit of the Lord has filled the inhabited world, and that which holds together all things has knowledge of voice', in place of: he has embraced the invisible and visible creation, the intelligible and the perceptible, and nothing of all things is without a share of his eternal oversight; for the holding together of all things shows this. And every voice, he says, he hears, as God being always in all things everywhere, and leading round every material disharmony into the fitting order, and both sparing and caring for the things made by him, inasmuch as he himself is by nature providence and wisdom, having passed through all things, as the Father. For who is the one having such knowledge? And Isaiah says thus: 'spirit of knowledge and godliness', and David sings to it: 'where shall I go from your face? and from your Spirit where shall I flee?' And the Master too, teaching that the Godhead of the Holy Spirit is not circumscribed by place, but is together both in heaven and on earth, having always furnished and furnishing all sufficiency to the creation, said in John: 'if you love me, keep my commandments; and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that the Spirit of truth may be with you, which the world cannot receive, it does not behold it nor know it; but you know it, because it remains beside you, and will be in you.' And so that it may become known that such testimonies too declare him as of the one limitless nature present everywhere: they handed down equal things about each of the two undefiled hypostases, Jeremiah on the one hand setting it out from God and Father: 'I fill heaven and earth, says the Lord'; and David about the Son in the 144th psalm (English 145) singing: 'and of his greatness there is no limit'; and Paul proclaiming about the same: 'the one who came down is himself also the one who went up above all the heavens, so that he might fill all things.' 6.3ν [Chapter title:] That he is incorruptible. The creation is not incorruptible once for all; but it admits corruption, the turning (copy-text: nourishment), which we also call change, as the prophecy says: 'the one making all things and refashioning them.' Having overheard which, the wise men of those outside say: dissolving them into themselves, and out of them again making them grow. For on the one hand the bodiless rational creation has corruption according to choice, God on the one hand having given it an abiding nature, and having set it up for the age and for the age of the age; but it on the other hand changing by its own choice and falling out into a worse allotment, and by this very [...]
pass_b_english: … reprobate, ungrateful and profane, having shown itself such by its own will. Scripture, for its part, nowhere says that the divine Spirit has a beginning; it honours him as “Spirit of God”, “from God”, “divine” and “holy”. Nor does it mark off, in the nature of the divine hypostases, a “first of all” and an “afterwards”. What dispute, then, is left about their being in the one unbegotten Godhead and in equal honour?
That he fills the world and holds all things together.

Nothing created fills the world, or holds all things together, and is present in all things. Even the intellectual powers have a limit and a fixed quantity; for these things belong to the Godhead alone. But the greatness of the Holy Spirit cannot be broken up and has no bound; it is always everywhere, through all things and in all things. By his Godhead he fills the world and holds it together, yet by his power he cannot be contained; he measures, but is not measured. “For God does not give the Spirit by measure,” as the Saviour says in John (John 3:34). So too in Wisdom, which runs: “For you love all things that exist, and loathe none of the things you have made; for you would not have fashioned anything if you hated it. How would anything have lasted, had you not willed it, or how would what you had not called have been kept? You spare all things, because all things are yours, Master, lover of souls, and your incorruptible Spirit is in all things” (Wisdom of Solomon 11:24-26; Wisdom of Solomon 12:1). Hence we rightly name God Father of all, though he is not our Father by nature, as he is the Father of his Only-begotten.

And again: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world, and that which holds all things together has knowledge of the voice” (Wisdom of Solomon 1:7). That is: he has embraced the invisible and the visible creation, the intelligible and the sensible, and nothing in all the world lacks a share in his eternal oversight; that is what “holding all things together” shows. And he hears every voice, the text means, since he is God, always present in all things everywhere. He brings all the disorder of matter round into its fitting order, and he spares and cares for the things made by him, since he is by nature providence and wisdom, passing through all things, as the Father does. For who is it that has such knowledge? Isaiah says: “a spirit of knowledge and godliness” (Isaiah 11:2). And David sings: “Where shall I go from your face? And from your Spirit where shall I flee?” (Psalm 139:7).

The Master too taught that the Godhead of the Holy Spirit is not bounded by place, but is at once in heaven and on earth, and has always supplied, and still supplies, every sufficiency to creation. So he said in John: “If you love me, keep my commandments. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that the Spirit of truth may be with you, whom the world cannot receive; it does not see him or know him. But you know him, because he abides with you and will be in you” (John 14:15-17).

And so that it may be known that such testimonies too declare him to belong to the one boundless nature that is present everywhere, the saints handed down the same things about each of the other two undefiled hypostases. Jeremiah, setting it out as from God the Father: “I fill heaven and earth, says the Lord” (Jeremiah 23:24). David, singing of the Son in the hundred and forty-fifth Psalm: “And of his greatness there is no end” (Psalm 145:3). And Paul, proclaiming the same Son: “He who descended is himself also the one who ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things” (Ephesians 4:10).

Creation is not incorruptible once and for all. It admits corruption, that is, the turning which we also call change, as the prophecy says: “He who makes all things and transforms them.” The wise men of the outsiders overheard this and say: “dissolving them into themselves, and making them grow again out of themselves.” For the bodiless rational creation has corruption by choice. lemmas.gloss: speak well of, honour with a title

choices.issue: Old draft garbled, mis-divided, wrong references
choices.choice: Retranslated the whole section from the Greek. The old English made the opening neuter participle (the reprobate creature of the previous section's sentence) into a 'private opinion' and turned 'Scripture nowhere says the Spirit has a beginning' into 'neither the Scripture saying that the Divine Spirit is a beginning'; it ran the 6.2 chapter title into the text under a bracket filler '[The opponent claims]' and read 'the intellectual powers have a limit' as the Spirit being 'the limit of the noetic powers'; it rendered τροφήν as 'nourishment'. References fixed: John 14:15-21 (the quotation is 14:15-17); 'the 40th Psalm' for Greek Psalm ρμδʹ = 144 (now Psalm 145:3); abbreviated Isa/Ps/Jer/Eph written out; 'Wisdom 11:24-26' and 'Wisdom 1:7' now 'Wisdom of Solomon', with Wisdom 12:1 added for the last line of that quotation; John 3:34 and Psalm 148:6 added. The chapter titles 6.2ν and 6.3ν now stand as their own paragraphs; '6.3' removed from the reading text; bracket fillers [it], [saying] and [The opponent claims] removed. Opens and ends mid-sentence as the Greek does.

choices.term: ἀδόκιμον, ἀχάριστον καὶ βέβηλον ἐξ οἰκείας γνώμης φανέν
choices.english: … reprobate, ungrateful and profane, having shown itself such by its own will
choices.why: The section opens mid-sentence; the neuter agrees with δημιούργημα at the end of the previous section (the first creature, Satan, who became wicked by his own choice). Only this section's words are translated, with a leading ellipsis.
55 is a printed page number in the copy-text; page debris, omitted.
The copy-text has the singular ὑποστάσεως after a plural article; the sense (and αὐτάς, 'their being', that follows) requires the plural.
Didymus quotes the opponents' ranking terms; kept as quoted terms.
Both words mean the world here; 'inhabited world' would be heavy in the chapter title and the Wisdom quotation.

choices.term: κατὰ τὴν θεότητα … κατὰ τὴν δύναμιν
choices.english: By his Godhead … by his power
choices.why: Two parallel 'according to' phrases; kept parallel.
The copy-text reads βληθέν ('thrown'); Wisdom 11:25 reads κληθέν ('called'), a one-letter difference. Translated as 'called'; see problems.

choices.term: γνῶσιν ἔχει φωνῆς … πάσης, φησίν, ἐπακούει φωνῆς
choices.english: has knowledge of the voice … he hears every voice, the text means
choices.why: Didymus explains the Wisdom phrase; φησίν marks his reading of the text, not a new quotation.
Greek neuter after πνεῦμα; English uses the personal pronoun for the Spirit throughout, as Didymus' own argument treats him as a Person.

choices.english: about each of the other two undefiled hypostases
choices.why: ἑκάτερος means each of two; the two are the Father and the Son, as the quotations that follow show. 'the saints' as subject of παρέδοσαν is drawn from the witnesses named (Jeremiah, David, Paul).

The copy-text reads τροφήν ('nourishment'), which makes no sense in a list of corruption and change; read as τροπήν ('turning'), the word Didymus uses for the same thing in the next section (τροπὴν ὑπομένει). See problems.

choices.english: the wise men of the outsiders
choices.why: οἱ ἔξω is the usual term for pagan (non-Christian) writers.

choices.term: στήσαντος αὐτὴν εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα, καὶ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τοῦ αἰῶνος
choices.english: established it for ever and ever (Psalm 148:6)
choices.why: Wording of Greek Psalm 148:6, applied to the rational creation; the KJV verse says the same.
The sentence runs on into the next section (τούτῳ φθειρομένης); only this section's words are translated.
